query: We are investigating a specific eutectic high entropy alloy (comprising Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni) that exhibits a dual-phase lamellar structure and suffers from catastrophic interfacial cracking and low ductility. The operating regime is room temperature uniaxial tension. Known failures include the strength-ductility trade-off and stress concentration at phase interfaces. Design constraints require maintaining the alloy composition while altering the microstructure to arrest interfacial cracking and promote uniform plasticity. Propose a high-intensity thermomechanical treatment hypothesis that could transform the lamellar structure into a patterned configuration, explain the predicted boundary conditions for success (e.g., specific temperature/pressure windows), and define a falsification experiment involving conventional hot isostatic pressing to isolate the effect of extreme pressure.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a high-intensity thermomechanical treatment (HITM) involving severe plastic deformation (SPD) followed by a controlled low-temperature anneal will fragment the continuous lamellar B2 phase into a patterned, discontinuous network of B2 precipitates within the FCC matrix, thereby arresting interfacial cracking and promoting uniform plasticity via coherent interface-mediated dislocation transmission.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi eutectic high entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar (approx. 2 μm spacing) fcc/B2 dual-phase structure.
generation.intervention: High-intensity thermomechanical treatment: Severe Plastic Deformation (e.g., Equal Channel Angular Pressing or High-Pressure Torsion) at room temperature to introduce high dislocation density and break lamellar continuity, followed by a short-duration anneal at 600-800°C to stabilize the fragmented B2 phase without coarsening.
generation.conditions: Deformation strain > 4 (true strain); Annealing temperature: 600-800°C; Annealing time: 1-4 hours; Atmosphere: Vacuum or inert gas to prevent oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Fragmented B2 phase forming a reticulated or discrete precipitate network within the continuous FCC matrix, replacing the continuous lamellar B2 phase.
generation.mechanism: Based on the principle that continuous ordered phases (B2) act as crack propagation paths and stress concentrators (PMC4145285::chunk::002::discussion::f8c841f9e4), the HITM breaks this continuity. The resulting discrete B2 interfaces, if coherent or semi-coherent, facilitate dislocation transmission and relieve stress concentrations similar to the SCCP mechanism in W-based HEAs (PMC10213035::chunk::000::abstract::2906c9eda2), while the discrete dispersion of the brittle phase prevents catastrophic interfacial cracking, analogous to the inverted microstructure strategy in refractory HEAs (PMC5995863::chunk::000::abstract::63aa5c975c).
generation.predicted_outcome: A 30-50% increase in room temperature tensile ductility (fracture strain > 15%) with a maintained or slightly increased yield strength (> 800 MPa), and the elimination of catastrophic interfacial cracking observed in the as-cast state.
generation.baseline: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 with 2 μm lamellar spacing, exhibiting low ductility and catastrophic interfacial cracking under room temperature tension.
generation.boundary: The treatment is effective only if the annealing temperature remains below the solvus temperature of the B2 phase to prevent dissolution, and the deformation strain is sufficient to fully fragment the lamellae without inducing amorphization or excessive grain growth.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty exists regarding the exact annealing temperature window required to stabilize the fragmented B2 phase without coarsening; the specific strain required to achieve the 'patterned' configuration without introducing voids is also uncertain. The transition from lamellar to patterned may be non-linear.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of AlCoCrFeNi samples: (1) As-cast (control), (2) Subjected to standard Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1200°C/207 MPa for 1 hour (to test if conventional HIP alone transforms the structure), and (3) Subjected to the proposed HITM (SPD + low-temp anneal).
measurements: Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to quantify lamellar continuity vs. discrete precipitate formation.
Room temperature uniaxial tensile testing to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and fracture strain.
Fracture surface analysis to identify crack initiation sites (interface vs. matrix).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the HIP-treated sample (2) shows no significant improvement in ductility or microstructural transformation compared to the as-cast sample, AND the HITM sample (3) fails to show a reduction in interfacial cracking or an increase in ductility compared to the as-cast sample.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. To verify this novel alloy design strategy, an industrial scale AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 ingot of ~2.5 kg in weight was prepared, as shown in Fig. 1a . The bulk AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 alloy exhibited an excellent castability with few casting defects, significantly differentiating with other bulk HEAs. The tensile test specimen was machined from the bulk alloy ingot and is shown in Fig. 1b . The cast microstructure of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 is shown in Fig. 2a . Even in such a bulk cast ingot, a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure characteristic of eutectic alloys was achieved. The inter-lamellar spacing was about 2 μm. The coupled grown two phases showed a clear compositional contrast, with the regions marked by A in Fig. 2b were rich in Co, Cr and Fe, while the regions marked by B were rich in Al and Ni (detailed compositional information given in Table 1 ). An enlarged microstructure given in Fig. 2c shows that dense nanoscale NiAl-rich precipitates (marked as B II ) occurred in the CoCrFe-rich region. As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.
